text: hey everybody why do most critical scholars  believe that james's speech at the end of
the jerusalem council in acts 15 is unlikely to  be historical has to do with james's quotation
of a passage from the hebrew bible it appears  to be amos 9 verses 11 through 12. but there
are some issues with this and james introduces  this quotation by referring to it as the words   of the prophets in the plural rather than just  the singular prophet amos but when we compare
acts 15 16 through 17 with amos 9 11 through  12 the picture comes into a bit better focus
uh the quotation of amos 9 11 in acts 15 16 is  not exactly what we find in amos it actually
seems to be drawing greek terminology and phrases  from other prophetic books like zechariah or
jeremiah or others and this is likely what was  known as an early christian testimonial which was
kind of a super quotation from the scriptures  where you take the terminology the words the
phrases from a bunch of different places and bring  them together into a more concentrated quotation
of the scriptures that would be more rhetorically  powerful easier to recognize so this may be why
the author of the book of acts has james introduce  this quotation not as the word of the prophet amos
but the words of the prophets because it is a  testimonial that brings us to the quotation of
amos 9 12 in acts 15 17. if you look at amos 9 11  through 12 this is about the restoration of the
tent of david and in verse 12 it says and they  will possess or take possession of the remnant
of edom so this is about the restoration of  the kingdom of david to its original size
which requires the reconquest of edomite territory  which was lost now what is quoted in acts 15 17
has absolutely nothing whatsoever to do with  edom or with conquest because two of the words
in amos 9 12 have been reread renegotiated  whether intentionally or otherwise the verb
yarash to inherit to take possession of has been  re-read as darash to seek after and the word edom
has been reread as adam human humanity so instead  of they shall take possession of the remnant of
edom the text reads the remnant of humanity shall  seek this is the greek translation of amos 9
12 this is what is in the septuagint but  because it has just renegotiated those two
words the sentence is grammatically incomplete our  transitive verb to seek does not have an object
in the septuagint but what's quoted in acts  15 17 provides an object we'll seek after
the lord so what we have in acts 15 16-17  seems to be an early christian testimonial
that's drawing from zechariah and jeremiah and  elsewhere to restate amos 9 11 combined with
an elaboration on the septuagint's renegotiation  of amos 9 12. so this is certainly something that
it is possible that a historical james could have  quoted in the jerusalem council in the mid-first
century ce but seems very unlikely not only  because christian testimonia were in circulation
in a later period but also because a quotation  from the septuagint that then builds on that
that septuagint quotation is far more likely to  be something that an author writing in greek at
a later time period would do rather than a person  engaged in a conversation in aramaic in jerusalem
with skeptical pharisees in the audience they  would have objected to james saying hey this
is the words of the prophets and they would have  said no it's not that has nothing to do with the
words of the prophets as we see right here this  is about reconquest of the land of edom and so   i have seen a number of different  arguments for why this is
can be historical and certainly it's possible but  on balance the preponderance of evidence would
indicate that the quotation in acts 15 verses  16 and 17 is most likely the production of an
author writing in greek specifically the  author of the book of acts it is unlikely to   have been something that the historical james  would have said during the jerusalem council
